course.title: Git/GitHub
course.description: A complete Git/GitHub course that progresses from Git's repository and commit model through staging, branches, merges, rebases, history recovery, remotes, pull requests, repository governance, GitHub Actions, security, repository hygiene, advanced maintenance, and release engineering. It combines command-line Git fluency with the collaboration and operational controls required for serious software repositories.
prerequisites: Basic familiarity with files, directories, and text editors.
learningOutcomes: Explain Git's working tree, index, commits, references, and graph.
Use branches, remotes, fetch, pull, push, merge, rebase, and conflict recovery safely.
Investigate and recover history with reflog and bisect.
Use stash, cherry-pick, tags, worktrees, hooks, attributes, and large-file strategies appropriately.
Collaborate through GitHub forks, pull requests, reviews, templates, and ownership.
Prevent and respond to credential leaks.
Design traceable releases, hotfixes, and rollback processes.
Complete a governed Git/GitHub repository workflow.

modules.title: Git Foundations
modules.description: Build a precise mental model of Git before using collaboration features.

lessons.title: Git's repository model
lessons.description: Git is a distributed version-control system. A repository contains objects, references, configuration, and an index; the working tree is the checked-out filesystem.
learningObjectives: Explain repository, working tree, index, commit, and reference roles.

notes.text: Git is a distributed version-control system. A repository contains objects, references, configuration, and an index; the working tree is the checked-out filesystem.

git status
git rev-parse --show-toplevel

practicals.title: Inspect a repository boundary
practicals.description: A focused exercise for the concept.
steps: Identify the working tree and .git directory.
practicals.solution:
git init demo
cd demo
git status
git rev-parse --show-toplevel
practicals.output: Git reports repository state and its top-level directory.

quiz.question: What is the index used for?
options: Selecting content for the next commit
quiz.answer: Selecting content for the next commit
quiz.explanation: The index is Git's staging area.

summary: Git is a distributed version-control system. A repository contains objects, references, configuration, and an index; the working tree is the checked-out filesystem.

lessons.title: Commits and snapshots
lessons.description: A commit records a project snapshot plus metadata and parent relationships. Commit history forms a directed graph.
learningObjectives: Describe commits as graph nodes and explain parent relationships.

notes.text: A commit records a project snapshot plus metadata and parent relationships. Commit history forms a directed graph.
git log --oneline --graph --decorate

practicals.title: Read a commit graph
practicals.description: A focused exercise for the concept.
practicals.solution: git log --oneline --graph --decorate --all
practicals.output: The graph shows commit ancestry.

quiz.question: What does a normal commit point to?
quiz.explanation: Commit objects record parent relationships.

summary: A commit records a project snapshot plus metadata and parent relationships. Commit history forms a directed graph.

lessons.title: Git configuration and identity
lessons.description: Git configuration has system, global, and local scopes. Author identity is part of commit metadata.
learningObjectives: Configure and inspect local identity without storing real credentials.

notes.text: Git configuration has system, global, and local scopes. Author identity is part of commit metadata.

git config user.name "Training Author"
git config user.email "training@example.invalid"

practicals.title: Configure local identity
practicals.description: A focused exercise for the concept.
steps: Create a test commit and inspect author metadata.
practicals.solution:
git config user.name "Training Author"
git config user.email "training@example.invalid"
git config --local --list
practicals.output: The repository has local identity settings.

quiz.question: Which scope affects one repository?
quiz.explanation: Local configuration applies to the current repository.

summary: Git configuration has system, global, and local scopes. Author identity is part of commit metadata.

lessons.title: Status, diff, and show
lessons.description: Git's inspection commands let you verify state before changing history.
learningObjectives: Compare working-tree, staged, and committed content.

notes.text: Git's inspection commands let you verify state before changing history.

git status
git diff
git diff --cached
git show HEAD

practicals.title: Audit a proposed commit
practicals.description: A focused exercise for the concept.
practicals.solution:
git diff
git add README.md
git diff --cached
git show --stat HEAD
practicals.output: The staged diff identifies exactly what will be committed.

quiz.question: Which command shows staged changes?
quiz.explanation: It compares the index with HEAD.

summary: Git's inspection commands let you verify state before changing history.

tasks.title: Create and audit a clean repository
tasks.description: Create a repository with a verified first commit.
tasks.problemStatement: The repository must have one useful README and a clean working tree.
tasks.objectives: Initialize, configure local identity, stage, commit, inspect.
tasks.requirements: Use only Git; do not edit .git manually.
tasks.hint:
git init
git config user.name "Training Author"
git config user.email "training@example.invalid"
printf '# Project\n' > README.md
git add README.md
git commit -m "docs: add project readme"
git status
git show --stat HEAD
tasks.solutionCode: This establishes the minimum safe Git lifecycle.

modules.title: Staging and Commit Craft
modules.description: Turn working-tree changes into deliberate, reviewable history.

lessons.title: Staging complete files and hunks
lessons.description: The index lets a developer choose precisely what enters the next commit.
learningObjectives: Stage files and selected hunks.

notes.text: The index lets a developer choose precisely what enters the next commit.
git add -p

practicals.title: Separate two changes in one file
practicals.description: The index lets a developer choose precisely what enters the next commit.
practicals.solution:
git add -p
git commit -m "docs: clarify usage"
git add -p
git commit -m "fix: correct behavior"
practicals.output: Two focused commits result.

quiz.question: Why use git add -p?
options: To select specific hunks for staging
quiz.answer: To select specific hunks for staging
quiz.explanation: Interactive staging selects hunks.

summary: The index lets a developer choose precisely what enters the next commit.

lessons.title: Commit message design
lessons.description: Git accepts arbitrary messages; teams can adopt conventions such as Conventional Commits to make intent machine-readable.
learningObjectives: Write specific subjects and recognize feat/fix/docs conventions.

notes.text: Git accepts arbitrary messages; teams can adopt conventions such as Conventional Commits to make intent machine-readable.
git commit -m "fix(api): reject empty input"

practicals.title: Improve three commit messages
practicals.description: Git accepts arbitrary messages; teams can adopt conventions such as Conventional Commits to make intent machine-readable.
steps: Replace vague subjects with specific intent.
Use a scope only when useful.
practicals.solution:
git commit -m "fix(api): reject empty input"
git commit -m "docs: clarify setup"
git commit -m "test: cover invalid input"
practicals.output: Messages communicate purpose.

quiz.question: What is Conventional Commits?
options: A commit-message convention layered on Git
quiz.answer: A commit-message convention layered on Git
quiz.explanation: It is a convention, not a Git requirement.

summary: Git accepts arbitrary messages; teams can adopt conventions such as Conventional Commits to make intent machine-readable.

lessons.title: Amending the latest local commit
lessons.description: Amend replaces the latest commit with a new commit object, so it is best used before shared history depends on the old object.
learningObjectives: Amend a forgotten file or message and identify the collaboration risk.

notes.text: Amend replaces the latest commit with a new commit object, so it is best used before shared history depends on the old object.

git add forgotten.md
git commit --amend --no-edit

practicals.title: Add an omitted file
practicals.description: Amend replaces the latest commit with a new commit object, so it is best used before shared history depends on the old object.
practicals.solution:
git add forgotten.md
git commit --amend --no-edit
practicals.output: The latest commit includes the file.

quiz.question: When is amend safest?
quiz.explanation: Amend rewrites the latest commit.

summary: Amend replaces the latest commit with a new commit object, so it is best used before shared history depends on the old object.

lessons.title: Restore and clean undo operations
lessons.description: Modern restore commands distinguish working-tree restoration from removing content from the index.
learningObjectives: Restore unstaged content and unstage without destroying working-tree edits.

notes.text: Modern restore commands distinguish working-tree restoration from removing content from the index.

git restore file
git restore --staged file

practicals.title: Undo one accidental edit
practicals.description: Modern restore commands distinguish working-tree restoration from removing content from the index.
practicals.solution:
git restore first.txt
git status
practicals.output: Only the selected file is restored.

quiz.question: What does restore --staged do?
options: It removes changes from the index
quiz.answer: It removes changes from the index
quiz.explanation: The working-tree edit can remain.

summary: Modern restore commands distinguish working-tree restoration from removing content from the index.

tasks.title: Build a coherent commit series
tasks.description: Separate mixed work into focused commits.
tasks.problemStatement: Documentation, behavior, and tests are mixed in the same working tree.
tasks.objectives: Use interactive staging and specific messages.
tasks.requirements: Stage by intent, not by file count.
tasks.hint:
git add -p
git commit -m "fix: correct input handling"
git add -p
git commit -m "test: cover invalid input"
git add -p
git commit -m "docs: clarify input rules"
tasks.solutionCode: The resulting history is easier to review and revert.

modules.title: Branching and Parallel Work
modules.description: Use branches and upstream relationships to isolate work without losing the shared graph.

lessons.title: Branches as movable references
lessons.description: A branch name points to a commit and advances when new commits are created on that branch.
learningObjectives: Create, switch, and inspect branches.

notes.text: A branch name points to a commit and advances when new commits are created on that branch.

git switch -c feature/reporting
git log --graph --all

practicals.title: Create a feature branch
practicals.description: A branch name points to a commit and advances when new commits are created on that branch.
steps: Create and switch to a branch.
practicals.solution:
git switch -c feature/reporting
git add .
git commit -m "feat: add reporting skeleton"
git log --graph --oneline --all
practicals.output: The feature branch advances independently.

quiz.question: What is a branch?
options: A movable reference to a commit
quiz.answer: A movable reference to a commit
quiz.explanation: A branch name identifies a commit tip.

summary: A branch name points to a commit and advances when new commits are created on that branch.

lessons.title: Tracking branches and upstreams
lessons.description: Local branches can track remote-tracking branches so push and pull can infer a destination.
learningObjectives: Inspect branch -vv and establish upstream.

notes.text: Local branches can track remote-tracking branches so push and pull can infer a destination.
git push -u origin feature/reporting

practicals.title: Establish an upstream
practicals.description: Local branches can track remote-tracking branches so push and pull can infer a destination.
practicals.solution:
git push -u origin feature/reporting
git branch -vv
practicals.output: The local branch records its upstream.

quiz.question: What does -u establish?
quiz.explanation: It records the remote branch used by later synchronization.

summary: Local branches can track remote-tracking branches so push and pull can infer a destination.

lessons.title: Branch naming and lifecycle
lessons.description: Branch names are references, so teams can adopt short-lived naming conventions and delete merged topic branches.
learningObjectives: Design branch names and safely delete merged branches.

notes.text: Branch names are references, so teams can adopt short-lived naming conventions and delete merged topic branches.

git branch --merged
git branch -d feature/reporting

practicals.title: Clean a merged branch
practicals.description: Branch names are references, so teams can adopt short-lived naming conventions and delete merged topic branches.
practicals.solution:
git branch --merged
git branch -d feature/reporting
practicals.output: The merged local branch is removed.

quiz.question: Why does -d check merge status?
quiz.explanation: The safe delete checks reachability/merge status.

summary: Branch names are references, so teams can adopt short-lived naming conventions and delete merged topic branches.

lessons.title: Remote-tracking branches
lessons.description: A remote-tracking name such as origin/main is a local reference to the last fetched state, not a live network object.
learningObjectives: Inspect and compare remote-tracking refs.

notes.text: A remote-tracking name such as origin/main is a local reference to the last fetched state, not a live network object.

git fetch origin
git branch -r
git log HEAD..origin/main

practicals.title: Inspect incoming history
practicals.description: A remote-tracking name such as origin/main is a local reference to the last fetched state, not a live network object.
practicals.solution:
git fetch origin
git log --oneline HEAD..origin/main
practicals.output: Incoming commits can be inspected before integration.

quiz.question: What is origin/main?
quiz.explanation: It records the state observed from the origin remote.

summary: A remote-tracking name such as origin/main is a local reference to the last fetched state, not a live network object.

tasks.title: Design a branch policy
tasks.description: Define a practical branch naming and cleanup policy.
tasks.problemStatement: The team needs feature, fix, and release work without long-lived uncontrolled branches.
tasks.objectives: Define names, merge expectations, and cleanup rules.
tasks.requirements: Keep protected branches separate from short-lived topic branches.
tasks.hint:
feature/<topic>
fix/<topic>
release/<version>
Policy: protect main; merge reviewed changes; delete merged topic branches.
tasks.solutionCode: The policy translates Git references into a predictable team workflow.

modules.title: Merging, Rebasing and Conflicts
modules.description: Integrate divergent work while preserving intended behavior and understanding history rewriting.

lessons.title: Fast-forward and three-way merge
lessons.description: A merge can move a branch directly when histories permit or create a merge commit when branches diverged.
learningObjectives: Predict merge results from a commit graph.

notes.text: A merge can move a branch directly when histories permit or create a merge commit when branches diverged.

git merge feature/reporting
git log --graph --oneline --all

practicals.title: Inspect a merge
practicals.description: A merge can move a branch directly when histories permit or create a merge commit when branches diverged.
practicals.solution:
git merge feature/reporting
git log --graph --oneline --decorate --all
practicals.output: The graph reveals the resulting topology.

quiz.question: When is fast-forward possible?
options: When the target is an ancestor of the source tip
quiz.answer: When the target is an ancestor of the source tip
quiz.explanation: No divergent target-side commit must be combined.

summary: A merge can move a branch directly when histories permit or create a merge commit when branches diverged.

lessons.title: Rebase and rewritten commit identity
lessons.description: Rebase replays commits onto a new base, creating new commit objects.
learningObjectives: Rebase a private branch and explain rewritten IDs.

notes.text: Rebase replays commits onto a new base, creating new commit objects.

git switch feature/reporting
git rebase main

practicals.title: Rebase a private topic branch
practicals.description: Rebase replays commits onto a new base, creating new commit objects.
practicals.solution:
git switch feature/reporting
git rebase main
git log --graph --oneline --all
practicals.output: The feature commits have new identities because their parents changed.

quiz.question: Why can rebase change commit IDs?
options: It creates commits with different parent relationships
quiz.answer: It creates commits with different parent relationships
quiz.explanation: Parent references contribute to commit identity.

summary: Rebase replays commits onto a new base, creating new commit objects.

lessons.title: Conflict anatomy and resolution
lessons.description: Git stops when it cannot safely combine overlapping changes; conflict markers expose the competing text.
learningObjectives: Resolve a conflict and stage the result.

notes.text: Git stops when it cannot safely combine overlapping changes; conflict markers expose the competing text.

<<<<<<< HEAD
current
=======
incoming
>>>>>>> feature

practicals.title: Resolve a controlled conflict
practicals.description: Git stops when it cannot safely combine overlapping changes; conflict markers expose the competing text.
steps: Create different edits to the same lines.
practicals.solution:
git status
# edit conflict markers away
git add conflicted.txt
git commit
practicals.output: The resolved file becomes the merge result.

quiz.question: What follows manual conflict resolution?
options: Stage the resolved file and finish the operation
quiz.answer: Stage the resolved file and finish the operation
quiz.explanation: Git records the resolution through the index.

summary: Git stops when it cannot safely combine overlapping changes; conflict markers expose the competing text.

lessons.title: Abort and continue integration
lessons.description: Merge and rebase provide explicit continuation and abort paths when integration cannot proceed.
learningObjectives: Use rebase --continue and --abort safely.

notes.text: Merge and rebase provide explicit continuation and abort paths when integration cannot proceed.

git add resolved.txt
git rebase --continue
# or
git rebase --abort

practicals.title: Practice aborting
practicals.description: Merge and rebase provide explicit continuation and abort paths when integration cannot proceed.
practicals.solution:
git rebase --abort
git status
practicals.output: The pre-rebase state is restored.

quiz.question: Which command abandons a rebase?
quiz.explanation: It restores the branch to the pre-rebase state.

summary: Merge and rebase provide explicit continuation and abort paths when integration cannot proceed.

tasks.title: Resolve a multi-file integration conflict
tasks.description: Integrate overlapping application and test changes.
tasks.problemStatement: Two branches changed related behavior and tests.
tasks.objectives: Resolve conflicts semantically, stage every resolved file, then run tests.
tasks.requirements: Treat each conflict as a behavior decision, not merely marker deletion.
tasks.hint:
git merge feature/update
# resolve files
git add src/ test/
git commit -m "merge: integrate update"
npm test
tasks.solutionCode: A correct resolution preserves intended behavior and passes validation.

modules.title: History, Debugging and Recovery
modules.description: Turn Git history into an investigation and recovery toolkit.

lessons.title: History search with log and show
lessons.description: Git history can be filtered by paths, messages, authors, and graph relationships.
learningObjectives: Locate a candidate change and inspect its patch.

notes.text: Git history can be filtered by paths, messages, authors, and graph relationships.

git log --oneline -- path/to/file
git show <commit>

practicals.title: Trace a file change
practicals.description: Git history can be filtered by paths, messages, authors, and graph relationships.
steps: Compare a commit with its parent.
practicals.solution:
git log --oneline -- path/to/file
git show <commit>
git diff <commit>^ <commit> -- path/to/file
practicals.output: The investigation identifies concrete changes.

quiz.question: Which command shows a commit patch?
quiz.explanation: show displays commit metadata and its patch.

summary: Git history can be filtered by paths, messages, authors, and graph relationships.

lessons.title: Blame as a change-tracing tool
lessons.description: Blame maps lines to commits and is useful for finding context, but it is not proof that the named author is responsible for a bug.
learningObjectives: Use blame to locate the commit that introduced a line.

notes.text: Blame maps lines to commits and is useful for finding context, but it is not proof that the named author is responsible for a bug.
git blame -L 20,40 src/app.js

practicals.title: Trace ownership of a line
practicals.description: Blame maps lines to commits and is useful for finding context, but it is not proof that the named author is responsible for a bug.
steps: Inspect the cited commit with show.
practicals.solution:
git blame -L 20,40 src/app.js
git show <commit>
practicals.output: Each line is associated with a commit in the current file state.

quiz.question: What is blame best for?
options: Tracing a line to a commit for context
quiz.answer: Tracing a line to a commit for context
quiz.explanation: It points you toward history; it is not a judgment of fault.

summary: Blame maps lines to commits and is useful for finding context, but it is not proof that the named author is responsible for a bug.

lessons.title: Reset versus revert
lessons.description: Reset moves references and can alter local history; revert records a new inverse commit and is suited to shared history.
learningObjectives: Choose reset or revert based on sharing and safety.

notes.text: Reset moves references and can alter local history; revert records a new inverse commit and is suited to shared history.

git reset --soft HEAD~1
git revert <commit>

practicals.title: Compare undo strategies
practicals.description: Reset moves references and can alter local history; revert records a new inverse commit and is suited to shared history.
steps: Use revert in a shared-style branch.
practicals.solution:
git reset --soft HEAD~1
git revert <commit>
practicals.output: Reset and revert have different history consequences.

quiz.question: Which is normally appropriate on shared history?
quiz.explanation: Revert avoids rewriting existing shared commits.

summary: Reset moves references and can alter local history; revert records a new inverse commit and is suited to shared history.

lessons.title: Reflog recovery
lessons.description: Reflogs record local reference movements and can reveal commits that a branch name no longer points to.
learningObjectives: Recover a lost local tip.

notes.text: Reflogs record local reference movements and can reveal commits that a branch name no longer points to.

git reflog
git switch -c recovery HEAD@{1}

practicals.title: Recover after an accidental reset
practicals.description: Reflogs record local reference movements and can reveal commits that a branch name no longer points to.
practicals.solution:
git reflog
git switch -c recovery HEAD@{1}
practicals.output: The recovery branch points at the prior reflog entry.

quiz.question: What does reflog record?
quiz.explanation: It records updates such as HEAD and branch movements locally.

summary: Reflogs record local reference movements and can reveal commits that a branch name no longer points to.

lessons.title: Stash for temporary work
lessons.description: A stash temporarily records working-tree/index changes without turning unfinished work into normal project history.
learningObjectives: Create, inspect, and apply a stash.

notes.text: A stash temporarily records working-tree/index changes without turning unfinished work into normal project history.

git stash push -m "wip"
git stash list
git stash pop

practicals.title: Shelve unfinished work
practicals.description: A stash temporarily records working-tree/index changes without turning unfinished work into normal project history.
practicals.solution:
git stash push -m "wip: investigation"
git stash list
git stash pop
practicals.output: The unfinished change returns to the working tree.

quiz.question: What is stash intended for?
quiz.explanation: It is a short-term shelving mechanism.

summary: A stash temporarily records working-tree/index changes without turning unfinished work into normal project history.

lessons.title: Cherry-pick for targeted transfer
lessons.description: Cherry-pick applies the change introduced by an existing commit onto another branch.
learningObjectives: Backport one self-contained fix.

notes.text: Cherry-pick applies the change introduced by an existing commit onto another branch.
git cherry-pick <commit>

practicals.title: Backport a fix
practicals.description: Cherry-pick applies the change introduced by an existing commit onto another branch.
practicals.solution:
git switch maintenance
git cherry-pick <fix-commit>
npm test
practicals.output: The fix appears as a new commit on maintenance.

quiz.question: What does cherry-pick transfer?
options: The changes introduced by selected commits
quiz.answer: The changes introduced by selected commits
quiz.explanation: It creates a new commit on the current branch.

summary: Cherry-pick applies the change introduced by an existing commit onto another branch.

lessons.title: Bisect for reproducible regressions
lessons.description: Bisect performs a binary search over commit history and is effective when a deterministic test can classify commits.
learningObjectives: Automate a regression search.

notes.text: Bisect performs a binary search over commit history and is effective when a deterministic test can classify commits.

git bisect start
git bisect bad
git bisect good <known-good>
git bisect run ./test.sh

practicals.title: Locate the first bad commit
practicals.description: Bisect performs a binary search over commit history and is effective when a deterministic test can classify commits.
practicals.solution:
git bisect start
git bisect bad
git bisect good <known-good>
git bisect run ./test.sh
git bisect reset
practicals.output: Git narrows the candidate set using the test result.

quiz.question: What does bisect require?
quiz.explanation: An unreliable test produces unreliable search results.

summary: Bisect performs a binary search over commit history and is effective when a deterministic test can classify commits.

tasks.title: Investigate and recover a regression
tasks.description: Use reflog to recover a moved reference and bisect to isolate a reproducible regression.
tasks.problemStatement: A disposable repository contains an accidental reset and a deterministic failing test.
tasks.objectives: Use reflog first, then bisect with the test command.
tasks.requirements: Do not rewrite shared history during the exercise.
tasks.hint:
git reflog
git switch -c recovered HEAD@{1}
git bisect start
git bisect bad
git bisect good <known-good>
git bisect run ./test.sh
git bisect reset
tasks.solutionCode: The exercise demonstrates reference recovery and evidence-based regression isolation.

modules.title: Remotes, Synchronization and Releases
modules.description: Synchronize local and remote histories deliberately and make release points traceable.

lessons.title: Remote names and fetch
lessons.description: Remote names identify configured repositories; fetch updates remote-tracking refs without integrating them.
learningObjectives: Inspect remotes and fetch safely.

notes.text: Remote names identify configured repositories; fetch updates remote-tracking refs without integrating them.

git remote -v

git branch -r

practicals.title: Inspect incoming changes
practicals.description: Remote names identify configured repositories; fetch updates remote-tracking refs without integrating them.
practicals.solution:
git remote -v

git log --oneline HEAD..origin/main
practicals.output: Incoming history is visible without changing the current branch.

quiz.question: What does fetch do?
options: Downloads updates and updates remote-tracking refs
quiz.answer: Downloads updates and updates remote-tracking refs
quiz.explanation: Fetch separates download from integration.

summary: Remote names identify configured repositories; fetch updates remote-tracking refs without integrating them.

lessons.title: Pull as fetch plus integration
lessons.description: Pull combines fetching with an integration strategy, so teams should choose explicit merge/rebase behavior.
learningObjectives: Explain pull --ff-only and pull --rebase.

notes.text: Pull combines fetching with an integration strategy, so teams should choose explicit merge/rebase behavior.

quiz.question: Why can pull surprise users?
options: It combines fetch with an integration step
quiz.answer: It combines fetch with an integration step
quiz.explanation: Pull is more than downloading.

summary: Pull combines fetching with an integration strategy, so teams should choose explicit merge/rebase behavior.

lessons.title: Push, rejection, and force-with-lease
lessons.description: A non-fast-forward push protects remote history. Force-with-lease rewrites only when the remote still matches the expected state.
learningObjectives: Handle a rejected push and explain force-with-lease.

notes.text: A non-fast-forward push protects remote history. Force-with-lease rewrites only when the remote still matches the expected state.

practicals.title: Recover from a rejected push

practicals.solution:

practicals.output: The push succeeds after local history includes the required remote ancestry.

quiz.question: Why is force-with-lease safer than force?
options: It checks the remote ref before rewriting
quiz.answer: It checks the remote ref before rewriting

summary: A non-fast-forward push protects remote history. Force-with-lease rewrites only when the remote still matches the expected state.

code.README.md:
# Governed Delivery Repository

A neutral Git/GitHub training repository demonstrating focused commits, pull requests,
ownership, CI, security controls, and traceable releases.

## Workflow
1. Create a short-lived feature branch.
2. Make a focused commit.
3. Run local tests and inspect the diff.
4. Open a pull request.
5. Pass required CI and review.
6. Merge according to repository policy.
7. Tag validated releases.

code.SECURITY.md:
# Security

Never commit credentials, tokens, private keys, or production configuration.

If a credential is exposed, revoke/rotate it, remove it from relevant pending/history
where appropriate, investigate downstream copies, and document remediation.

Workflow files under `.github/workflows/` are security-sensitive and require review.
code.RELEASE.md:
# Release Runbook

1. Confirm review and required CI checks.
2. Identify the exact commit to release.
3. Create an annotated version tag.
4. Publish release notes from actual changes.
5. Deploy the artifact built from that commit.
6. Verify production.
7. If necessary, redeploy a known-good artifact/tag.
8. Propagate source hotfixes back to active development.
code.CONTRIBUTING.md:
# Contributing

Use short-lived feature/fix branches and focused commits.

Examples:
- feat: add filtering
- fix: reject empty title
- test: cover validation

Before a pull request:
- run npm test
- inspect git diff
- verify no secrets are present
- describe testing and risk

project.explanation: The application is intentionally small: `src/index.js` and its tests provide a real change surface without distracting from Git/GitHub. `.gitignore` and `.gitattributes` establish repository hygiene. CODEOWNERS and the PR template make review responsibilities and required context explicit. The CI workflow tests multiple Node versions and grants the workflow token only contents-read permission. SECURITY.md treats credentials and workflow files as security-sensitive. RELEASE.md separates source-control state from deployment state and provides a rollback-oriented process. The student is expected to configure protected branches/rulesets and then execute a real pull-request workflow on an authorized repository. The project therefore assesses both Git command fluency and GitHub governance/automation competence.
